newsitem.title: FRANCE: New Gaullist party chief known for unorthodox ways.
newsitem.headline: New Gaullist party chief known for unorthodox ways.

text.p: Philippe Seguin, the new leader of France's Gaullist Rally for the Republic (RPR), has risen in politics by challenging the powers that be and expressing aloud what most politicians keep to themselves.

Soon after the French right's crushing defeat in a June 1 parliamentary election, the populist former National Assembly speaker defied outgoing prime minister Alain Juppe and launched a high-profile campaign to oust him as RPR leader.

The quest mirrored an earlier campaign in which he bucked the RPR establishment to lead a nationalist campaign against the Maastricht Treaty in a 1992 referendum, coming within a whisker of turning voters against European union.
Now he faces his biggest challenge -- and an huge political opportunity. That is to try to lead the dispirited and divided RPR out of the political wilderness and back into power.
The opportunity is the possibility of a challenge to Gaullist President Jacques Chirac's re-election in 2002, when the president's current seven-year term runs out.

Seguin, a longtime Juppe rival who consistently scores among France's most popular politicians in opinion polls, has come to be widely viewed as a potential rival to Chirac despite his fervent pleas for unity.
His victory was "not a new step in a personal adventure," he insisted in a speech to the special party congress which chose him as RPR leader.
"In these moments, our thoughts, our affection and our loyalty must go to the person who has united us, towards Jacques Chirac," Seguin said.

RPR activists have been working overtime to shield Chirac from blame for his decision to call a snap election despite the huge National Assembly majority enjoyed by a right-wing coalition allying the RPR and the centrist Union for French Democracy (UDF).
Chirac had hoped to renew his majority for the last five years of his term so he could count on its support in carrying France into European economic and monetary union.
His gamble proved disastrous. Instead of winning a renewed mandate, the French right was swept from power by an alliance of Socialists, Communists and Greens.
Almost immediately, the right fell into quarrelling and infighting over who was responsible. In the end, Juppe bore most of the blame, giving Seguin his opening.
A huge bearlike figure with a deep voice and sagging bags under his eyes, the 54-year-old former university lecturer insists he has put his Euro-scepticism behind him.
He now says he supports the shift to the euro single currency and further European integration.
Seguin was born in Tunis in 1943 and never knew his father, who died in World War Two when he was a baby.
He studied politics and literature in southern France and graduated from the elite Ecole Nationale d'Administration civil service school to become a Finance Ministry inspector.
An adviser to President Georges Pompidou in 1973, he joined the cabinet of centrist prime minister Raymond Barre in 1977.

Elected to parliament for Epinal, near the German border, in 1978, he became deputy speaker of the National Assembly and opposition spokesman on major issues following the 1981 Socialist election victory. He is still mayor of Epinal.
Twice married, he has four children.
